description: We’re a five-person team mixing data science, software engineering, and 3D design. Our lead was a 2023 Space Apps Global Nominee with a Unity space simulator. We want to turn real NASA data, like NISAR radar or Mars terrain, into immersive 3D experiences that make hidden changes on a planet visible.
summary: Ourea turns NASA-ISRO NISAR radar into a flood-season child-safety tool for Vietnam's Mekong Delta. Nearly 2,000 children drown in Vietnam every year, many in flooded fields and canals right next to home. The flood comes with the monsoon, when clouds hide the ground from camera satellites: photos near our radar passes were up to 98% cloud. NISAR's radar sees through. From three 2026 NISAR passes over Đồng Tháp, we mapped water spreading from 26.6% to 55.3% of a 4,000 km² area (1,335 km² of new flood water) and found about 28,100 children under five living within about 100 m of it. An open, weighted score ranks 64 communes and their hamlets by where to check first. A 3D app that runs in any browser, on a laptop or a phone, shows it: a guided story, a village watching the water arrive, ranked lists with reasons, walking routes to the nearest day care and school, a ready-to-send message for the commune office and flood-text sign-up. Officials can send protection that already works, like supervised flood-season day care, to the right places after every pass. Đồng Tháp is our team lead's father's hometown.
details:
What it does. Ourea answers one question after every NISAR radar pass: where is flood water now close to homes, schools and young children, and which communes should we check first? It is built for provincial education and child-protection offices and commune officials who decide where to open flood-season childcare points and where to send safety teams.

How it works. (1) We download NISAR Level-2 GCOV radar images from NASA's Alaska Satellite Facility: track 047 descending, frame 083, passes on 11 Jul, 28 Aug and 3 Oct 2026. This is NISAR's first public data, which NASA may still correct. (2) We map water. Calm water reflects the radar away from the satellite, so it looks dark; pixels darker than a cut-off (HH below −13 dB, picked with Otsu's method) count as water. New flood water is water on land that was dry on 11 Jul, the start of the season. (3) We count children under five (WorldPop), homes and schools (OpenStreetMap) within about 100 m of new flood water, and rank every commune and hamlet with a visible score: 35% homes near flood water, 25% young children near it, 20% land newly flooded since 11 Jul, 20% schools near flood water. (4) We find walking routes to the nearest day care and school on OpenStreetMap roads and on Google Maps, and check every 20 m against the radar and ground heights (FABDEM), so a raised dike beside the water is not counted as flooded. (5) A Unity 3D app shows it all in the browser over real terrain (Copernicus GLO-30, FABDEM), buildings (GHSL) and trees (ETH canopy height), fed by a Cloudflare Worker API, with flood texts sent by Twilio.

What we found. Water on our 4,000 km² tile rose from 26.6% to 39.3% to 55.3%. Children under five near new flood water rose from 21,700 (28 Aug) to 28,100 (3 Oct) of 81,100; 18 of 94 schools sit near it. The physical driver: the Mekong at Tân Châu rose from 1.04 m in July to a peak near 3.2 m around 21 Sep, then fell, yet water on the land kept spreading because the floodplain fills and drains slowly. Dikes and the rice calendar decide which fields fill. 2026 was a low-flood year; the river never reached the first flood-alarm level.

How sure are we. We compared NISAR's water map with Sentinel-1 radar taken one day later. NISAR found 98–99% of the water Sentinel-1 saw, but it also marked about twice as much area as water, mostly rice fields: NISAR's longer wave sees water under the crop that Sentinel-1 misses, and some fields are flooded on purpose. Changing any weight in the score by half keeps 7 to 10 of the same top 10 hamlets. The list does depend on the start date: it ranks water that arrived after the dry season, and a later start date asks a different question. Details and scripts: docs/VALIDATION.md in our repo.

Polarization and frequency. NISAR sends its radar wave flat (horizontal) and listens two ways. HH (sent and heard flat) shows open water best. Flooded rice and trees can look bright in HH, because the wave bounces off the water and then off the stems back to the satellite. HV (sent flat, heard upright) responds to the leaves themselves. Using both is how we plan to tell rice paddies from river flood. NISAR's 24 cm L-band wave passes through cloud and crops better than Sentinel-1's 5.5 cm C-band.

Impact. In UNICEF and Alliance for Safe Children research, young children in supervised village day care had over 80% fewer drowning deaths, and WHO recommends day care for under-6s to prevent drowning. Ourea does not replace that protection; it points it at the right communes, every 12 days, for free, under any cloud. The app ends in an action: a ranked list with reasons, a ready-to-send message for the commune office (Vietnamese or English, shareable to Zalo), and a list of hamlets, routes and schools to print or download for a meeting.

Creativity. A guided story flies from the globe into the delta and walks through the passes; "Follow the water in one town" turns houses red as new water comes within 100 m; a wipe compares the cloudy photo with the radar. Routes to day care and school: walking routes from a check-first hamlet, drawn on the 3D map and in a Google Maps panel, show how much of each route is under water or on low ground beside new flood water; raised dikes don't count. The best route is labelled "least water on that pass", never "safe". Calm music and water sounds rise with the flood, and the app works on phones as well as laptops.

Tools. Python (rasterio, numpy, pystac-client), Unity 6 (C#, URP, WebGL), Cloudflare Workers and Pages (JavaScript), Google Maps JavaScript and Routes APIs, OpenStreetMap routing, Twilio, GitHub Actions, Claude.

Limits and safeguards. Radar maps water, not children. Some October water is rice fields flooded on purpose, so our October numbers may be a little high; separating rice from flood is our next step. NISAR's data is an early release that NASA may still correct. Canals narrower than about 30 m (one radar pixel) are missed. Child counts are WorldPop estimates, not a census, and OpenStreetMap is missing some schools. 2026 was a low-flood year. We never label a place or route as safe, and we use no personal data about children.
